Artwork & materials

The opening painting and chapter-specific historical scenes are contemporary AI-generated artistic reconstructions produced with Higgsfield’s GPT Image model. They are not documentary photographs or authentic medieval objects. Papal likenesses are artistic interpretations. Fátima is a devotional reconstruction featuring the three shepherd children. Mexico c.1750 and France c.1880 are separately dated illustrative communities, not records of particular events.

The wooden Rosary, crucifix, prayer counters, were constructed programmatically for this project. Lepanto now uses a coherent illustrated battle composition; earlier procedural ships and their separate water plane are no longer shown. Annunciation and Fátima combine separate image layers with spatial geometry; their figures are not volumetric characters. Earth uses NASA Blue Marble daylight imagery and a NASA Earth Observatory cloud composite. Credit NASA/GSFC Scientific Visualization Studio and Reto Stockli. Clouds are a historical composite, not live weather. Three.js is distributed under the MIT license. Typography uses Google Fonts’ Cormorant Garamond and Manrope; system serif and sans-serif fallbacks are provided.

The medieval counting cord is representative artwork informed by London Museum prayer-bead evidence, not a replica. Close Earth views use NASA Blue Marble 8K/4K surface layers. Authentic St Peter’s and Fátima photographs carry linked author and Creative Commons licenses in their destination panels.

Audio consists of original synthesized, organ-like ambient tones. It is optional and initially off.

Images & Credits

The Rosary Today uses the supplied Golden Light at the Grotto image, displayed in full.

The Marian Psalter and John PaulII chapel portrait are generated artistic reconstructions. The Perpetual Help medal reproduces the public-domain historical icon: source. It is shown complete, without repainting.

30 of32 shrine destinations have verified actual-place photographs. Elele and Nyaunglebin remain without a verified reusable photograph. Toulouse and Cologne are present-day place illustrations, not photographs of medieval events. Lepanto remains a labeled artistic reconstruction.
